grant.abstract: This project investigates improving the spectrum efficiency in battleground mobile adhoc networks (MANETs) with dynamic spectrum access (DSA). To achieve informationdominance in battlegrounds, one key is the ability to efficiently use the electromagneticspectrum. Cognitive radio (CR) and DSA are innovative ways to improving spectrum efficiencyin communications. Although experiments have been done on the potentials of DSA inbattlegrounds, many challenges still need to be addressed before DSA can really perform inbattlegrounds. One such challenge is fast, accurate, and engery-efficient spectrum sensing inbattlegrounds, and another is fast rendezvousing of battle units in a radio channel that is sensedavailable at a given time. Because of the highly dynamic spectrum activities in a battleground,DSA with slow or inaccurate spectrum sensing or slow rendezvousing will be impractical in abattleground. Most existing spectrum sensing and rendezvousing schemes are designed targetingcivil networks, and are not suitable for battleground MANETs because of their inaccuracy,latency, or energy consumption. Our basic approach to the spectrum sensing and rendezvousingchallenges in battleground MANETs is spectrum access assistance (SAA) based on primitiveasynchronous communication. With our knowledge on priority scheduling in MANETs usingprimitive tone-based communication, in this project we will investigate fast, accurate, andenergy-efficient spectrum sensing that incorporates SAA from primary users (PUs). Based on thesame approach, we will also investigate fast rendezvousing that allows battle units in abattleground to quickly rendezvous in a radio channel.

grant.title: A New Form of Antenna Diversity for Improved Spectral and Energy Efficiency in Wireless Networks
grant.abstract: It is well-known that antenna diversity techniques, ranging from simple antenna switching to highly optimized multiple input - multiple output systems, substantially improve the reliability and capacity of wireless communications. Typical forms of antenna diversity are spatial, pattern, and polarization diversity. We propose a new diversity method, antenna impulse response diversity (AIRD), which uses multiple co-located antennas that have direction-dependent impulse responses. Preliminary work suggests that the new method has many of the advantages of spatial diversity without the need for an electrically large footprint. In contrast with pattern diversity, the new approach uses omnidirectional patterns which maintain large diversity gain in multicast applications limited by the weakest peer. In its simplest form using selection diversity, AIRD can work with any transceiver architecture without modification, and consumes negligible additional power. Most importantly for the SpecEES program objectives of spectral efficiency and energy efficiency, antenna diversity reduces the transmit power required to obtain a given quality of service, thus lowering the ambient interference level and increasing availability for all users of the spectrum. We propose to (a) develop multiport antennas suitable for AIRD, (b) fully characterize the performance in multipath fields, (c) evaluate performance in realistic wireless networks through both multilayer network modeling and field tests using both measurement grade and standard commercial wireless network adapters, (d) produce publicly available performance data, antenna designs, and models suitable for system level design. The project team is a collaboration of two specialists, one in wireless network protocols, and one in electromagnetics and antenna design.

Answer Record electrical activity from participants brain using scalp recorded electroencephalogram (EEG) to access fear of a food product due to possible adverse effect on human body and the effect of that fear on the purchase likelihood of that product. EEG will be used to validate the self accessed ratings provided by the participant. Many factors influence food choice and consumption behavior (Koster 2009), fear is one of them (Laros and Steenkamp 2004). Past studies have shown fear appeals concerning genetically modified food (Laros and Steenkamp 2004), consumers’ fear (neophobia) towards food technologies (Verneau et al. 2014), and knowledge of fear and genetically modified food (Boccia et al. 2018). However, studies about food choice motivated by fear have not yet been examined through neuroscientific methods. In this study, we are interested in measuring the level of fear of consumers with regards to food choice when the food in question lacks safety for consumption. The purpose of this study is not only to measure consumers’ fear level but also try to identify consumer awareness or knowledge in consumer decision-making process in their food purchase intentions. In applying neuroscientific methods to measure the level of fear the effectiveness of different marketing strategies may be evaluated through consumers observing stimuli depicting different types of food (Khushaba et al. 2012). N. Masood et al (2019) investigated EEG patterns for dual-stimuli induced human fear emotional state [1]. They have used two types of stimulus, one is self-recalling of a fearsome event and the other one video clips from horror movies. The authors have employed common spatial pattern (CSP) as preprocessing method to select optimal EEG channels that will provide best separability of the types of task also called as class and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) as a classifier for the experiment. Emotiv EPOC has been used for EEG data collection from 15 young healthy participants. The experiment was divided into two-part, part one is designed for self-induced stimulus where the subject was asked to recall an event that induces fear in them, part two is for movie clips-based stimulus. The target was to study whether different stimulus for the same emotional state shows any correlation. The authors have employed 6 bandpass filter for 6 frequency ranges (delta 1-3 Hz, theta 4-7 Hz, alpha 8-13 Hz, low gamma 31- 50 Hz, high gamma 50-100 Hz, whole EEG range 1-100 Hz). ICA was employed to remove independent components with large weights over frontal or temporal areas, together with corresponding temporal courses showing eye movement or muscle movements were removed. CSP was employed to extract features and finally, LDA was used to classify self-induced vs video-induced fear states. The average accuracies were in the range of 54.86 to 72.74 for different frequency band signals.

grant.abstract: CNS Core: Small: RUI: Network State Conservation in Systems with Spectrum Coexistence Project Summary Overview: The proliferation of wireless devices has been straining the limited radio spectrum in recent years. The spectrum shortage problem will deteriorate as the ideas of Internet of things and smart communities are gaining acceptance. Spectrum coexistence becomes one important approach to improving spectrum efficiency. In systems with spectrum coexistence, communication and networking protocols need to coexist and collaborate to make spectrum constantly busy. This project investigates methods improving protocol efficiency for secondary users in spectrum coexistence systems. One important direction of the investigation is the impact of a cognitive-radio physical layer on the upper layers, such as the medium access control sub-layer and the transport layer. A cognitive-radio physical layer coupled with dynamic spectrum access may interrupt the activities at an upper layer at any given time, which can be costly in terms of spectral and energy efficiency. For example, when a cognitive-radio physical layer interrupts the ACK transmission in a RTS-CTS-DATA-ACK cycle of the IEEE 802.11 DCF, the energy and spectrum used for accomplishing the RTS-CTS-DATA exchange are totally wasted, impairing both spectral and energy efficiency in the network. This type of waste of resources may also occur in other protocols and at other upper layers in a spectrum coexistence system. For example, a smoothly running TCP cycle may be terminated by the cognitive-radio physical layer, resulting in otherwise successful data packets being retransmitted. On one hand, a secondary user must vacate a band as soon as the primary user needs it. On the other hand, a secondary user may waste a significant amount of energy and spectrum when it abruptly terminates its current or scheduled transmission and thus disrupts a protocol cycle. The proposed project investigates the spectral and energy impact of a cognitive-radio physical layer on the upper layers, and propose new network architectures and protocols to reduce or avoid such impact in spectrum coexistence systems. Intellectual merit: The proposed project investigates methods improving the protocol efficiency for secondary users in spectrum coexistence systems. Existing methods usually rely on the prediction of primary user’s traffic patterns in improving the protocol efficiency for secondary users, but it is intrinsically difficult to predict the primary user’s traffic arrivals and the duration of each arrival. Instead of relying on predicting the primary user’s traffic patterns, this project, based on protocol state conservation, redesigns the protocols of the secondary users to minimize the impact of the primary user on the secondary users. In addition, this project uses cross-layer collaboration in improving the protocol efficiency for secondary users. Although the basic approach of cross-layer design is not new in communications and networking research, the coupling of spectrum access assistance with state conservation across layers is a new method for improving spectral and energy efficiency in spectrum coexistence systems. In the implementation of this new method, new network architectures and protocols will need to be investigated, and new insights will be discovered in dynamic spectrum access in terms of spectral and energy efficiency. Broader impacts: The proposed project will benefit the society as a whole as well as some underrepresented minority groups in STEM. Spectrum and energy are two types of resources that are critical to a modern society. The spectrum resource becomes more strained every day, while pollution from energy consumption causes serious problems for the environment. The proposed project will improve both spectral and energy efficiency in wireless networks which are becoming ubiquitous. The proposed project will save a significant amount of energy consumed by future wireless networks. The saved energy will reduce emissions from electricity generation and benefit the environment. Besides its likely significant impact on the society as a whole, the project will promote STEM education among minority groups with its hiring and training of underrepresented minority students in STEM. The majority of students at UTRGV are Hispanics, who are underrepresented in STEM. We will actively recruit Hispanic students on the campus in the project. Our recruiting efforts will be facilitated by the resources available at UTRGV, such as the ADVANCE program funded by NSF and the Office of Engaged Scholarship & Learning, both of which promote STEM education for Hispanics. Key words: [Wireless Networks][Network Protocols][Performance, Spectrum Coexistence][Dynamic Spectrum Access]

grant.title: Non-invasive real-time microwave sensing of blood glucose concentration
grant.abstract: The proposed project aims to investigate and develop a non-invasive microwave sensing system for real time blood glucose concentration detection. Success of the project will not only benefit to those diagnosed type-1 and type-2 diabetes patients who need constant detection of their blood glucose level, but will also dramatically benefit to those potential pre-type-2 diabetes people that constant monitoring of their glucose level is of equal importance. Most of the studies on the non-invasive detection of glucose concentration are in vitro test only focusing on the glucose solution alone. The proposed project aims at in vivo non-invasive microwave detection of glucose concentration with interfering noises from the surrounding tissues. Major challenges have been predicted, including the interfering noises from the other tissues and the temperature effect. And we have planned the innovative strategies to overcome both. This project will develop both determinate and artificial neural network (ANN) statistical methods for the recognition of glucose concentration, to take the advantage of the self-evolutionary nature of the artificial neural network algorithm and reduce the detection variance from the interfering noise.

grant.title: Data Collection and Transmission for Large-scale and Long-lasting Soil Monitoring (Intent Letter)
grant.abstract: Soils are fundamental resources for humanity and economic prosperity. It is essential for the human to understand soil processes and maintain the health of soils, otherwise food production cannot be sustained and living environment can become hostile. One key to maintaining soil health is the ability to monitor the soil in a large geographic area and for a long time. To obtain accurate and timely soil measurements in a large geographic area for a long time, wireless underground sensor networks (WUSN) are likely the only feasible method. It is impractical for wired soil sensors to cover a large geographic area. Not only are the wires connecting wired soil sensors difficult to deploy, but also they may easily become interference to the use of the soil. On the other hand, remote sensing such as satellite imaging provides no or inaccurate data for many soil measurements. Wireless soil sensors are much easier and cheaper to deploy than wired sensors, and they can also provide accurate soil measurements. However, when wireless sensors transmit frequently, their life spans will be short because frequent wireless transmissions drain their batteries quickly. This is particularly true for underground soil sensors because an underground wireless channel introduces high signal attenuation while offering little bandwidth [1][2].

Distributed Leader-Following Tracking Control of Heterogeneous Uncertain Systems: A Distributed Immersion and Invariance Approach
grant.abstract: Distributed output tracking control of multiple systems plays an important role in many civilian and military applications where cooperation of multiple systems need work cooperatively. However, distributed controller design is challenging because 1) for each system the available information is the states/outputs of its own and its neighbors and 2) each system may be nonlinear and has uncertainty. In order to solve this challenging control problem, the following three research problems are proposed to be studied in this proposal: 1) distributed output tracking control of multiple heterogeneous uncertain linear systems, 2) distributed output tracking control of multiple heterogeneous nonlinear systems, and 3) distributed output tracking control of multiple heterogeneous uncertain nonlinear systems. To solve the above three research problems, a general multiple-step distributed immersion and invariance controller design (DIICD) approach will be proposed. Then, it is proposed to study how to solve each research problem with the aid of the proposed DIICD approach and other techniques. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed research results, experimental study will be conducted by implementing the proposed control laws in the multi-robot testbed in the PI's research laboratory. Based on the experimental results, the proposed distributed control laws will be improved accordingly. Intellectual Merit: The cooperative control of multiple identical linear systems has been extensively studied in the past decade and fruitful results have been obtained. However, these results cannot be applied to solve the leader-following tracking problem of multiple heterogeneous uncertain systems with limited information of its neighbors. This project will solve the leader-following tracking control problems of multiple heterogeneous systems with different assumptions on the dynamics and uncertainty in each system. The intellectual merits of this proposal are as follows: 1. a novel distributed immersion and invariance controller design approach is proposed for the leader-following tracking control problem; 2. the leader-following tracking control problem of multiple heterogeneous uncertain linear systems is solved; 3. the leader-following tracking control problems of multiple heterogeneous nonlinear systems with/without uncertainty are solved; and 4. the proposed controller design procedures can be applied to the distributed cooperative control problems of many practical control problems, such as flocking of mobile robots, formation control of unmanned aerial vehicles, etc. Broader Impacts: The research has significant impact in civilian, homeland security, and military applications where multiple systems work cooperatively. The research also has impact on the fields of biology, economics, physics, and computer science. The research plan will be integrated into an education plan including 1) undergraduate and graduate education. The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is a predominantly Hispanic institute. The PI will mentor minority students and female students through his research. The PI will develop a graduate course and an undergraduate course which are related to this project; and 2) broader dissemination of the research results. The research results will be published in journals and conference proceedings. The PI will also work closely with his industrial partners to transfer research results.

grant.title: Dynamic Spectrum Access in Battleground MANETs
grant.abstract: In this project we investigate dynamic spectrum access (DSA) in battleground mobile ad- hoc networks (MANETs). For achieving information dominance in battlegrounds, one key is the ability to innovatively use the electromagnetic spectrum. Cognitive radio (CR) and DSA have been proposed as innovative ways to improve spectrum efficiency in communications. Although experiments have been done on the potentials of DSA in battlegrounds, many challenges still need to be addressed before DSA can really perform in battlegrounds. One such challenge is fast, accurate, and energy-efficient spectrum sensing in battlegrounds, and another is fast rendezvousing of battle units in a radio channel that is sensed available at a given time. Due to the highly dynamic spectrum activities in a battleground, DSA with slow or inaccurate spectrum sensing or slow rendezvousing will be ineffective. Existing spectrum sensing and rendezvousing schemes are designed, in general, targeting civil networks, and are not suitable for battleground MANETs because of their inaccuracy, latency, or energy consumption. Our basic approach to the spectrum sensing and rendezvousing challenges in battleground MANETs is spectrum access assistance (SAA) based on primitive asynchronous communication. With our knowledge on priority scheduling in MANETs using primitive tone-based communication, in this project we will investigate fast, accurate, and energy-efficient spectrum sensing that incorporates SAA from primary users (PUs). Based on the same approach, we will also investigate fast rendezvousing that allows battle units in a battleground to quickly rendezvous in a radio channel.

grant.title: Network State Conservation in Dynamic Spectrum Access
grant.abstract: Overview: The proposed project is on improving spectral and energy efficiency in dynamic spectrum access via cross-layer collaboration. The proliferation of wireless devices has been straining the limited radio spectrum in recent years, particularly in heavily populated areas. The spectrum shortage problem will deteriorate as the ideas of Internet of things and smart communities are starting to gain attention and acceptance. Although cognitive radio and dynamic spectrum access may alleviate the spectrum shortage problem, they may aggravate the energy shortage problem of wireless devices powered by batteries due to the required constant channel sensing. Simultaneously addressing spectral efficiency and energy efficiency in dynamic spectrum access is thus critical. One perspective to this problem is to study the impact of a cognitive-radio physical layer on the upper layers, such as the medium access control sub- layer. A cognitive-radio physical layer coupled with dynamic spectrum access may interrupt the activities at an upper layer at any given time, which can be costly in terms of spectral and energy efficiency. For example, when a cognitive-radio physical layer interrupts the ACK transmission in a RTS-CTS-DATA- ACK cycle of the IEEE 802.11 DCF, the energy and spectrum used for accomplishing the RTS-CTS- DATA exchange are totally wasted, impairing both spectral and energy efficiency in the network. If this type of energy and spectrum waste caused by a cognitive-radio physical layer can be reduced or avoided, the spectral and energy efficiency in the cognitive radio network will significantly improve, as shown by the data in the proposal. On one hand, a secondary user must vacate a band as soon as the primary user needs it. On the other hand, a secondary user may waste significant energy and spectrum when it abruptly terminates its current or scheduled transmission and disrupts a communication cycle. The proposed project will investigate the spectral and energy impact of a cognitive-radio physical layer on the upper layers, and propose new network architectures and protocols to reduce or avoid such impact for improving spectral and energy efficiency in dynamic spectrum access. Intellectual Merit: The proposed project investigates cross-layer collaboration for improving spectral and energy efficiency in dynamic spectrum access. Although the basic approach of cross-layer design is not new in communications and networking research, the coupling of spectrum access assistance with state conservation across layers is a new method for improving spectral and energy efficiency in dynamic spectrum access. In the implementation of this new method, new network architectures and protocols will need to be investigated, and new insights will be discovered in dynamic spectrum access in terms of spectral and energy efficiency. Broader Impacts: The proposed project will benefit both the society and underrepresented minority groups in STEM. Spectrum and energy are two types of resources that are critical to a modern society. The limited spectrum resource becomes more strained every day, while pollution from energy production or consumption causes serious problems for the environment. The proposed project will improve both spectral and energy efficiency in wireless networks which are becoming ubiquitous. Global public Wi-Fi hotspots have been growing at a high speed in recent years, while global Wi-Fi traffic has been growing even more rapidly than other IP traffic. With the fast growing Wi-Fi traffic, the proposed project will save billions of kWh of electricity a year in the future because of improved energy efficiency in Wi-Fi networks. The saved energy will reduce the CO2 equivalent emissions by tens of thousands of tons a year from reduced electricity generation. The reduced emissions, meanwhile, will have the potential to save hundreds of human lives and prevent thousands of serious illnesses a year. Besides its likely significant impact on the society, the project will promote STEM education among minority groups with its hiring and training of underrepresented minority students in STEM. The majority of the students at UTRGV are Hispanics, who are underrepresented in STEM. We will actively recruit Hispanic students in the project. Our recruiting efforts will be facilitated by the resources available at UTRGV, such as the ADVANCE program funded by NSF and the Office of Engaged Scholarship & Learning, both of which promote STEM education for Hispanics.

grant.sponsor: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) DHS Science and Technology Directorate (S&T) Center of Excellence (COE) Center for Cross-Border Threat Screening and Supply Chain Defense – Center Lead

grant.abstract: One key in fast response to biological threats is to detect any threat quickly and report it quickly. Any delay in detecting or reporting a threat may result in irreversible consequences. DHS is funding numerous efforts to develop sensors for biological detection. When these sensors are deployed widely on or around the borders, they have to be networked for quickly reporting positive detection. In the scenario of an emergency of biologic detection, one challenge is to make sure that the sensor or sensors detecting the threat be able to have the highest priority in using the spectrum for reporting the detection data without delay. One technique that can be studied for this purpose is cognitive radio. Cognitive radios are able to adapt their operating parameters, such as frequency, power, and modulation, to the radio environment they constantly sense. When sensors and other nodes sharing the spectrum are equipped with cognitive radios, they become intelligent in using the spectrum and thus can be designed to yield to sensors detecting biologic threats. In this project we plan to study how cognitive radios can be applied in networks of biologic sensors so that sensors detecting threats will have the highest priority in using the spectrum and report the detection without being delayed. We already have some research results on cognitive radio networks and thus are prepared and qualified to conduct the project.

grant.title: The Impact of a Cognitive Radio Physical Layer in Combat Cognitive Radio Networks
grant.abstract: In this project we investigate the efficient use of the electromagnetic spectrum in naval combat and the impact of the physical layer change on the upper layers. To achieve information dominance, one key is the ability to innovatively use the electromagnetic spectrum in various areas such as surveillance, communications, and navigation. Cognitive radio (CR) has been proposed as an innovative way to improve spectrum efficiency. CRs are expected to be able to adapt their operating parameters, such as frequency, power, and modulation, to the radio environment they constantly sense. In combat there are priority tiers in using the spectrum, and thus some users may be assigned as the primary users, while some others will be the secondary users, as in the case of dynamic spectrum access of cognitive radios. In dynamic spectrum access, secondary users adopting cognitive radios share the spectrum with the primary users. Equipped with cognitive radios, the secondary users can determine at a given time if the primary users are actively using the spectrum. When the primary users are active, the secondary users back off. However, when the primary users are inactive, the secondary users can share the spectrum. In this way the spectrum can be used not only efficiently but also with priority enforced, which will likely be key for information dominance in future naval combat. Since in combat we still want the secondary user network to be effective, one important question in this scenario of cognitive radio networks is how the cognitive radio physical layer would impact on the secondary user network as a whole. We propose the abstracted network concept in cognitive radio networks and the use of a Markov chain model in analyzing the impact of the primary users on the secondary user network as a whole.

grant.abstract: The proposed project aims to study and develop the chirped pulse microwave sensor for chemical and biological trace gas detection. Potential detectable species include automobile gas emission detection, poisonous and pollution gases, etc. Many molecules have strong and characteristic rotational transitions in the microwave frequency region. The relative long wavelength of microwave radiation allows it to propagate further away than infrared radiation. The microwave technique is known to be highly sensitive to detect this kind of radiation. These properties make spectroscopic sensing of chemical species highly feasible in this frequency range. grant.title: The Development of an Industrial Assessment Center for South Texas
grant.sponsor: Department of Energy (DOE), Office of Energy Efficiency & Renewable Energy (EERE)
grant.abstract: The four counties in deep south Texas known as the Rio Grande Valley are home to one of the fastest growing populations and one of the fastest growing manufacturing sectors in the state of Texas and world. The region is known as the Rio Grande Valley because it is located on the northern banks of the Rio Grande River which serves as the international boundary between the United States and Mexico. The Rio Grande Valley is also home to the second largest federally certified Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI) of higher education in the United States, the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). Approximately 90% of the more than 25,000 UTRGV students are Hispanic. The UTRGV College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) has been recognized for the quality of its academic programs and the numerous partnerships and collaborations that its faculty have established with more than 100 entities in its service area including manufacturers, local governments, economic development councils, two year institutions of higher education and not-for-profit organizations. The undergraduate degrees that the CECS awards in civil engineering, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, manufacturing / industrial engineering and computer science engineering are all accredited by the Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology (ABET). There is a tremendous need for the creation of the South Texas Industrial Assessment Center (South Texas IAC). In spite of the Rio Grande Valley’s rapidly growing population and the growing manufacturing sector the closest Industrial Assessment Center (IAC) to deep south Texas is 350 miles away. The development of the South Texas IAC will provide industrial energy assessments to small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs) that previously did not have access to such no-cost energy assessments. Through the provision of these industrial energy assessments the South Texas IAC has the potential of assisting manufacturers to save millions of dollars each year in energy and water management costs. The proposal to develop a South Texas Industrial Assessment Center (South Texas IAC) described herein is made possible because of a number of CECS engineering faculty who possess the requisite expertise and willingness to work with 20 UTRGV engineering students to carry out twenty industrial assessments per year. The faculty participating in the activities being proposed herein represent all of the departments in the CECS including electrical engineering, manufacturing and industrial engineering, civil engineering, and mechanical engineering. The diversity of faculty members’ areas of specialization and their various departmental affiliations in the CECS will provide students with an appreciation of the cross disciplinary nature of industrial energy assessments. The diversity of faculty will also ensure that engineering students throughout the CECS will become aware of the existence of the South Texas IAC and will have the opportunity to participate in the assessment activities as well as internships and research projects that come about as a result of the creation of the South Texas IAC. As manufacturing enterprises in the Rio Grande Valley become aware of the tremendous financial benefits that accrue to them from the energy assessments offered through the South Texas IAC it is anticipated that small and large manufacturers alike will contribute to the financial viability of the South Texas IAC after grant funds expire.

grant.abstract: Fiber-reinforced geopolymer concrete with non-structural multifunction is suggested in this proposed project as an alternative construction material that has potential to cope with pressing challenges such as climate change and deterioration of modern infrastructures. Production of high CO2 emissions and low ductility are the shortcomings of conventional Portland cement concrete. The use of geopolymer concrete can substantially reduce CO2 emissions with improved durability. However, the complex and sensitive relations between multiple factors and mechanical performance of geopolymer hinders its standardization and widespread use. On the other hand, while fiber reinforcement in concrete is known to be an effective way to engineer the desired tensile/flexural properties, its application to geopolymer concrete is in the research stage. The proposed project aims to fill the technical gaps for the practical use and standardization of high-performance fiber-reinforced geopolymer by using AI-driven machine learning models and providing basic knowledge to engineer its performance. The data on the combined effects of geopolymer ingredients, fiber reinforcement, and other factors such as aggregate and curing conditions on strength, ductility, and internal pore structures will be collected through literature review and the proposed experimental program and will be analyzed using AI-driven machine learning tools to find the multiparameter relations. The project also investigates three potential multifunctional applications – damage sensing, strain sensing, and permeable reactive barrier – using advanced measurements including electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), electrical impedance tomography (EIT), and X-ray tomography (X-ray CT).

grant.abstract: The objective of the proposed project is to develop a nondestructive tool for evaluating the internal structures of concrete using 3D Electrochemical Impedance Tomography (EIT). The proposed EIT will generate 3D conductivity maps of cementitious composites and is expected to identify internal flaws/cavities, rebars, and microcracks. Concrete is the second most used material after water in modern civilization, and the evaluation of internal damage is critical for structural safety. The proposed idea is that flaws and rebars alter the conductive path in concrete, and internal structural maps can be constructed by monitoring the changes in electrochemical properties. EIT for concrete is an emerging nondestructive technique combining Impedance Spectroscopy and Tomography, but the application of EIT for concrete has not been well established yet. Upon success, the EIT allows real-time safety monitoring of concrete structures, and its application can be expanded to detect other damages such as underground sink holes.

An Optimized Laser-Induced Graphene-Based Electrochemical Biosensor Modified With Graphene-Conductive Ink for Alpha-Fetoprotein Detection
presentation.event: ASME 2024 International Mechanical Engineering Congress and Exposition (IMECE2024)
presentation.abstract: In this work, a label-free electrochemical immunosensor was fabricated for the detection of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) based on Laser-Induced Graphene (LIG) and modified with developed graphene polyaniline (G-PANI) ink. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a prominent biomarker for the diagnosis of primary liver cancer. For the prevention and treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), it is essential to ensure the accurate detection of AFP. The performance of our designed immunosensor was evaluated by differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) and Chronoamperometry (CA) techniques to detect cancer proteins in the phosphate buffer saline (PBS) and serum. Both electrochemical analyses in different concentrations of AFP resulted in a linear relationship between peak current and the logarithmic plot of the concentrations with a correlation coefficient, R 2 = 0.99. The limit of detection was also calculated to be ~0.73 ng/mL in the range of 4 ng/mL-500 ng/mL. The nearly identical current outputs in the DPV measurements were obtained consecutive ten times which represents the sensor’s stability with an RSD of 1.66%. Furthermore, the performance of the fabricated sensor in more complex biological environments was studied by detecting AFP in human serum (H4522). The current response was linearly proportional to the AFP concentration in serum samples. The results showed that the proposed immunosensor can be successfully used to detect AFP in PBS and undiluted human serum.

presentation.title: Improvement of laser-induced graphene-based electrochemical biosensors through graphene-conductive polymer ink coating for sensitive detection of alpha-fetoprotein
presentation.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of primary liver cancer and is the sixth most commonly occurring cancer worldwide with the second-highest mortality rate [1] [2]. Since the 1970s, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) has been used as a prominent biomarker for the diagnosis of HCC. But AFP is electrochemically inactive, thus, detecting AFP is unreliable for early detection of HCC [3]. In this study, we demonstrated the highly sensitive detection of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) by developing an electrochemical biosensor using Kapton film. The electrochemical sensor was fabricated by laser scribing technique which is a one-step method that does not require any oxidative acid synthesis route or chemical vapor deposition (CVD) to obtain graphene structure which reduced the cost tremendously [4]. The laser-induced graphene (LIG) electrodes were modified with developed graphene polyaniline (G-PANI) ink to effectively enhance the detection of electrical signals. The peak potential voltage difference was 600μV for the bare electrode, while after modifying with the ink the difference was reduced to 260 μV which indicates a 56% change. Therefore, the electrocatalytic effect of the electrode surface and electrochemical sensor signal was improved after modifying the electrode with ink. To evaluate the performance of the sensor, differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) techniques were performed in phosphate buffer saline (PBS) buffer with ferro-ferricyanide as the redox probe. For the DPV method, a significant surge in peak current was observed, increasing from 9.2 microamperes at a concentration of 20 pg/mL to 13.6 microamperes at 400 pg/mL which satisfied the fact that increasing the concentration of AFP, led to a higher number of analytes available for electron transfer, thus resulting in the observed current enhancement. The nearly identical current outputs in the DPV measurements were obtained consecutive 15 times which represents the sensor’s stability with an RSD of 3.69% and exhibits high reproducibility (RSD=12.15%, N=5). The obtained EIS result showed good linearity in charge transfer resistance change (coefficient of determination, R2= 0.87) with the AFP concentration increment in the range of 20 pg/mL - 400 pg/mL, and the limit of detection (LOD) was 146 pg/mL at a signal-to-noise ratio of 3, indicating the sensor's sensitivity. The range was selected due to demonstrate high sensitivity in the picogram range and has the potential to cover the entire physiological range for a healthy adult. The specific selectivity of the sensor was evidenced by obtaining a random current peak when both AFP and estrogen were introduced simultaneously on the surface of the sensor. For both electrochemical techniques, a similar coefficient of determination was found from the calibration curves, suggesting that the fabricated biosensor offers high selectivity to the determination of AFP biomarker.

presentation.title: Selective and Sensitive Determination of Dopamine in a Novel Gear Shaped Screen-Printed Electrode Modified With G-Pani Ink
presentation.event: ASME 2024 International Mechanical Engineering Congress and Exposition (IMECE2024)
presentation.abstract: Now-a-days electrochemical sensors are used to detect various analytes in bodily fluids. The electrodes of these sensors can be modified with various designs and particles. In our paper, we developed a novel gear-shaped electrode. The cyclic voltammetry (CV) analysis shows that the novel design has improved active surface area by 57% than without gear design. This novel design was fabricated as a screen-printed electrode using laser-induced graphene. Moreover, the novel shaped sensor was modified with polyaniline (G-PANI) ink to enhance the performance of the sensor. The physiochemical properties of the developed sensor were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). The modified electrode was used to detect dopamine (DA). Dopamine is an important catecholamines neurotransmitter which is known as “happy hormone”. It regulates various important body functions. But an abnormal range of dopamine in bodily fluid may lead to various diseases i.e., Parkinson disease, Alzheimer’s disease etc. This sensor can detect dopamine within the linear range of 0.1-10 μM, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.077μM (R2=0.98). Cyclic voltammetry, Electrical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) and chronoamperometry were also used to evaluate the performance of the sensor, in phosphate buffer saline (PBS) buffer with ferricyanide as the redox probe. The gear-shaped design has shown good repeatability and reproducibility. It has also shown a good selectivity in a ternary mixture of Uric Acid (UA) and Dopamine.

presentation.event: 2020 IEEE International Symposium on Antennas and Propagation and North American Radio Science Meeting
presentation.abstract: Abstract — Non-invasive blood sugar measurement attracts more and more attention in recent years, given the increase in diabetes-related complications and inconvenience in the traditional ways using blood droplets. In this paper, we present a study on the use of machine learning algorithms to determine glucose concentration based on the microwave scattering parameters (S 11 ) measured on the glucose solution with various concentrations. Dielectric parameters were extracted appropriately based on the modified Debye dielectric dispersion model from the measured broadband S 11 , and utilized as the features to create a large dataset by adding various Gaussian noises. Machine learning algorithms were then used to classify glucose concentrations ranging from pure water to 1000 mg/dL. A perfect 100% glucose concentration classification accuracy has been achieved. The study suggests a proposing way to develop the non-invasive glucose detection method using big data machine learning.

Comparison of Two Synthesis Methods to Deposit Silicon Nitride (Si3N4) thin films.
presentation.abstract: Silicon nitride thin film is a well-known kind of material in semiconductor industries. These films are used in important applications such as protective layers; insulators for optical devices, etc. It is also an important material in microelectronics due to its high resistivity, higher dielectric constant compared to silicon dioxide, mechanical strength, and chemical inertness. It is used as a gate insulator in thin film transistors that are in flat panel displays. In this work we have fabricated Silicon Nitride (Si3N4) thin films using RF magnetron sputtering method using Si3N4 Target. P-doped, N-doped Si wafers, sapphire wafers and glass plates are used as substrate material. We will also fabricate Silicon nitride thin films with Si target and N2 as process gas. It will be cost effective because Si targets are cheaper than Si3N4 targets. To compare the sputtered grown samples from both recipes, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) will be employed. Both high and low temperatures will be used for depositions so that we can find out the optimum conditions for silicon nitride deposition with highest purity possible. Silicon nitride films are mainly prepared by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD).
